item.title: OpenAI Releases Findings on 377 Math Problems, Further Roiling Field
item.description: After a previous solution angered mathematicians, the company characterized the new release as being more responsive to concerns about A.I. disrupting research.
item.dc:creator: Kenneth Chang and Siobhan Roberts
item.media:description: For 10 of the findings, OpenAI provided summaries of how the A.I. model came up with its solution. The average result took about three hours of computing, the company said.

item.title: Nobel Prize in Chemistry Is Awarded to Henri Kagan and Kenso Soai
item.description: The Nobel Committee recognized them for solving a century-old mystery about how molecules with mirror images can emerge in nature.
item.dc:creator: Cassandra Vinograd
item.media:credit: Fredrik Sandberg/TT News Agency, via Reuters
item.media:description: Henri Kagan and Kenso Soai are awarded the 2026 Nobel Prize in Chemistry during a news conference at the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences in Stockholm, on Wednesday.

item.title: The Start-Up That Wants to Build ‘Microrobots’ With A.I.
item.description: Atomic Machines is training artificial intelligence on materials and designs — and then using it to build tiny physical devices.
item.dc:creator: Cade Metz
item.media:credit: Christie Hemm Klok for The New York Times

item.title: Nobel Prize in Physics Is Awarded to Francis Halzen for Work on Neutrinos
item.description: The Nobel Committee honored Francis Halzen for his “vision and scientific leadership” of a telescope within the ice at the South Pole.
item.dc:creator: Aurelien Breeden and Katrina Miller
item.media:credit: Christine Olsson/TT News Agency, via Reuters
item.media:description: The Nobel Committee praised Francis Halzen’s “vision and scientific leadership” at the IceCube Neutrino Observatory, a research project at the South Pole.

item.title: What Are the Biggest Questions in Science Today? 100 Scientists Weigh In.
item.description: We asked 100 scientists about unsolved problems in their fields. They sent back provocations — on the origins of life, the possibilities for human progress and much more.
item.dc:creator: Bill Wasik
item.media:credit: Photo illustration by Jane Stockdale for The New York Times

item.title: Are Babies Conscious?
item.description: By pinpointing when it begins in young humans, scientists hope to better understand what consciousness is, and how it arises, in all of us.
item.dc:creator: Carl Zimmer

item.title: In Race With U.S., China Struggles to Recruit Foreign A.I. Researchers
item.description: China’s booming artificial intelligence sector has given local researchers good reason to remain in the country, but it has yet to lure overseas scientists despite a government push.
item.dc:creator: Zeyi Yang
item.media:description: Chinese A.I. companies like Deepseek and Moonshot have made a name for themselves internationally. But China still struggles to recruit foreign researchers.

item.title: Melting Swiss Glaciers Release Archaeological Treasures
item.description: Archaeologists are scouring mountain passes as artifacts from a bygone world all but tumble out of Switzerland’s shrinking ice.
item.dc:creator: Raymond Zhong, Giacomo d’Orlando and Mira Rojanasakul
item.media:description: Fragments of wood found recently around a fast-melting ice patch in the Swiss Alps.

item.title: Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine Is Awarded for Discoveries in Neuroscience
item.description: Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel were recognized for their work on light-gated ion channels and optogenetics, a technique that uses pulses of light to activate neurons in the brain.
item.dc:creator: Carolyn Y. Johnson and Leo Sands
item.media:description: Thomas Perlmann, the secretary general of the Nobel Committee, speaking at the Karolinska Institute in Stockholm on Monday.

item.title: U.S. Formally Seeks Information From Russia About Possible Plague Death
item.description: The lack of details from the Russian authorities has unnerved U.S. officials and others around the world.
item.dc:creator: Paul Sonne and Edward Wong
item.media:description: The entrance to the grounds of the anti-plague institute in Irkutsk, Russia, on Wednesday. An employee of the institute died of a mysterious pneumonia.

item.title: Supreme Court Hears Boulder Climate Case
item.description: Monday’s arguments were highly technical. A decision about whether the case could move forward isn’t expected until June or July.
item.dc:creator: David Gelles
item.media:description: Demonstrators outside the Supreme Court on Monday.

item.title: Energy Firms Try to Squeeze More Power Out of Old Nuclear Plants
item.description: It takes a long time to build new nuclear plants. So, some U.S. companies are looking to get more electricity out of reactors that already exist.
item.dc:creator: Brad Plumer and Rebecca F. Elliott
item.media:description: Constellation Energy, the nation’s largest nuclear power plant operator, said it would spend more than $4.3 billion to refurbish 11 reactors at six plants in Illinois, Pennsylvania and New Jersey.

item.title: Why Cities and States Are Fighting Climate Change in Courtrooms
item.description: Faced with a president who has called global warming a hoax, officials have filed dozens of suits against oil companies to try to cover the costs of extreme weather.
item.dc:creator: Karen Zraick and Claire Brown
item.media:description: The case now before the Supreme Court could affect dozens of others. Protesters gathered on Monday as the court heard arguments.

item.title: Texas Pediatricians Face Paxton Investigations for Vaccinating Children
item.description: Ken Paxton, the Texas attorney general and Republican Senate candidate, has alleged a sprawling profit-driven conspiracy. Pediatricians say the accusations are an attempt at intimidation.
item.dc:creator: Christina Jewett
item.media:credit: Kaylee Greenlee for The New York Times
item.media:description: Dr. Rachel examining a patient in Texas last month.

item.title: Nobel Prizes 2026: What to Know
item.description: The recipients of the six awards in science, literature, economics and peace work are being announced this week.
item.dc:creator: The New York Times
item.media:description: A Nobel Prize medal awarded in 1998. Six Nobels are given each year.

item.title: Scientists Warn of Another Unseen Risk From Fire: Ozone
item.description: Small particulates sent up by wildfires are a well-documented health hazard. But recent research finds that ground-level ozone is now on the rise, too.
item.dc:creator: Clayton Dalton
item.media:description: Manhattan’s skyline obscured by Canadian wildfire smoke on June 7, 2023.

item.title: A Supreme Court Battle Over Climate Change Begins
item.description: The justices are about to hear a lawsuit that could determine whether the oil industry faces billions of dollars in liability for damages caused by global warming.
item.dc:creator: Karen Zraick
item.media:credit: Mark Makela for The New York Times
item.media:description: Boulder has sued Exxon and Suncor saying they should help pay for the damage caused by global warming in the state. A Suncor refinery in Colorado last month.

item.title: These Birds Are Louder Than Elephants, Jackhammers and Chain Saws
item.description: A new study has identified two species of Brazilian birds, the bare-throated bellbird and the red-legged seriema, as the loudest in nature.
item.dc:creator: Taylor Mitchell Brown

item.title: F.D.A. Found Cyclospora During Taylor Farms Inspection in Mexico
item.description: The discovery adds strong evidence that the outbreak that sickened thousands over the summer originated in a grower’s field or processing facility.
item.dc:creator: Christina Jewett, Alice Callahan and Caroline Hopkins Legaspi
item.media:credit: Fred Ramos for The New York Times
item.media:description: Over the course of the summer, the cyclospora outbreak linked to Taylor Farms caused nearly 13,000 illnesses, 570 hospitalizations and two deaths in 21 states.

item.title: California Sues to Block Trump From Weakening Fuel Economy Rules
item.description: The lawsuit is the 97th the state has filed against the Trump administration over the past year and a half.
item.dc:creator: Brad Plumer
item.media:credit: Stella Kalinina for The New York Times
item.media:description: Traffic in Los Angeles. California led other states to sue the Trump administration on Friday over new fuel efficiency standards.

item.title: Scientists Untangle the Biology of an ‘Undruggable’ Cancer Gene
item.description: Found in 70 percent of cancers, the gene is seen as a grand orchestrator, but has been surprisingly difficult to stop.
item.dc:creator: Carolyn Y. Johnson

item.title: The MacArthur ‘Genius’ Studying Sea Ice Secrets
item.description: A climate scientist was one of 20 recipients of a “no-strings-attached” $800,000 stipend.
item.dc:creator: Claire Brown
item.category: MacArthur, John D and Catherine T, Foundation
item.media:credit: Chang W. Lee/The New York Times
item.media:description: Marika Holland’s work has revealed that ecosystems are at risk because sea ice is declining.

item.title: Prosecutors Cannot Revive Reflecting Pool Case Against Ex-Olympian, Judge Rules
item.description: A charge against David Hearn was dismissed “with prejudice” because of President Trump’s attempts to influence the case.
item.dc:creator: Clarence Williams
item.media:description: A renovation of the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool has been plagued with problems.

item.title: How Did Christa Pike Survive Two Lethal Injections of Pentobarbital?
item.description: A catheter carrying the drug may not have delivered the doses to Ms. Pike’s bloodstream, experts said. The drug itself may have been degraded.
item.dc:creator: Benjamin Mueller and Shaila Dewan
item.media:description: Emergency vehicles leaving Riverbend Maximum Security Institution after the failed execution of Christa Pike.

item.title: States Sue Over Trump’s Repeal of Climate Rules for Power Plants
item.description: The mostly Democratic-led states say that the E.P.A. acted unlawfully when it erased Biden-era limits on carbon dioxide from coal- and gas-fired plants.
item.dc:creator: Brad Plumer
item.media:credit: Benjamin Rasmussen for The New York Times
item.media:description: President Trump has pushed to dismantle many federal policies that aim to tackle climate change, including Biden-era rules that limited planet-warming emissions from power plants.

item.title: A Hacking Competition Shows the Power of China’s Approach to A.I.
item.description: The winner of a cybersecurity contest prevailed by relying on an ‘open weight’ Chinese model — another sign that available A.I. systems could already be too powerful to easily regulate.
item.dc:creator: Cade Metz
item.media:credit: Avishag Shaar-Yashuv for The New York Times
item.media:description: Pavel Gurvich, the chief executive of the cybersecurity company Tenzai. Mr. Gurvich’s firm won the HackerOne contest by using a freely available Chinese A.I. model.

item.title: Cornell’s Jane Doe Said She Was Given Ketamine. Here’s How the Drug Works.
item.description: Ketamine is a short-acting anesthetic that can have hallucinogenic effects. It is becoming more easily available, and some experts fear misuse is increasing.
item.dc:creator: Andrew Jacobs
item.media:description: Ketamine can have a hallucinogenic effect at certain doses.

item.title: Clues to Why a Breakthrough Pancreatic Cancer Drug Eventually Stops Working
item.description: Researchers are asking why patients, like former Senator Ben Sasse, inevitably develop resistance to the drug daraxonrasib.
item.dc:creator: Gina Kolata
item.media:credit: T.J. Kirkpatrick for The New York Times
item.media:description: Researchers are studying why patients, like former Senator Ben Sasse, eventually develop resistance to the drug daraxonrasib.

item.title: Viper Image That Caused Alarm in California Was A.I.-Generated
item.description: A Gaboon viper, a venomous snake native to equatorial regions of Africa, was supposedly photographed in a tree in Santa Ana, Calif. How could that be? Well, it turns out it wasn’t.
item.dc:creator: Victor Mather
item.media:description: This is a real Gaboon viper. One that was supposedly photographed in a tree in Santa Ana, Calif., was fake.
